I hear your frustration, and I want to acknowledge that this is one of the deepest and most painful questions a person can ask. When children suffer, it doesn't feel like a theological puzzle to be solved; it feels like a tragedy that demands an honest answer.

Based on Christian perspectives, there are a few different ways this is approached, though they may feel complex when faced with real pain:

*   **Human Freedom and Choice:** One perspective is that God gives human beings freedom. Because people are free to choose, some choose to do evil and corrupt the good God created. In this view, the suffering of children is not God's fault, but the result of humans choosing to commit harmful acts (EveryStudent, [https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).
*   **The Presence of Sin and Natural Law:** Other suffering is attributed to the general presence of sin in the world or the way natural laws work. For example, accidents and diseases happen to both the innocent and the guilty because we live in a world where these things are a reality (Sightline Ministry, [https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).
*   **Limited Human Understanding:** Some argue that our perspective is too limited to see the "wider framework" God is working within. They use the analogy of a child undergoing a painful surgery; the child doesn't understand why their parents allow the pain, but the parents have a reason that the child cannot yet comprehend (thelife, [https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-2](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-2)).
*   **God’s Solidarity in Suffering:** A central point in Christianity is that God did not remain distant from suffering. Through Jesus, God entered human form and suffered "beyond all comprehension" to show that He is with those who suffer and that He has a plan to eventually end suffering (thelife, [https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3); Cru, [https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html)).

I realize these answers may still feel like they don't fully address the "why" in a way that satisfies the heart, especially when the suffering is so innocent. Please know that it is okay to be angry or to struggle with these answers.

I hear your frustration, and I want to acknowledge that what you're asking is one of the hardest and most painful questions anyone can face. When a child suffers, an intellectual explanation often feels inadequate or even insulting because the pain is so visceral.

While I don't have a single answer that will take away that pain, I can share how different perspectives within the Christian tradition attempt to address this. They don't all agree, and they offer different ways of looking at the problem:

*   **The Role of Human Freedom:** One perspective is that God gives human beings freedom to make their own choices rather than controlling them. This freedom means that people can choose to do evil and cause suffering to others. In this view, it is not God's fault when people choose to corrupt the good He created, but rather a result of human choice (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html).
*   **A Broken World:** Another view is that suffering is a reality of living in a world where sin exists. This includes not only the sins of individuals but also the natural laws of the world (like gravity or disease) that can cause accidents and tragedy for anyone, regardless of whether they are "good" or "bad" (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this).
*   **Limited Human Understanding:** Some suggest that our perspective is simply too limited to understand God's reasons. Much like a small child might not understand why a parent allows a doctor to perform a painful surgery to save their life, humans may be unable to see how God's wider purposes or "providence" might eventually work through even the most horrific evils (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-2).
*   **A God Who Suffers With Us:** Rather than just providing an explanation, some find hope in the idea that God does not remain distant from suffering. In the Christian faith, Jesus is seen as God entering into human suffering directly. The belief is that by suffering Himself, He shows that He is not indifferent to our pain, but is "with us" in it (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3; Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this).

I know these aren't "easy" answers, and they don't change the reality of the suffering you are pointing to. If you want to talk more about any of these specific points, or if there's a different angle you're struggling with, I'm here to listen.

I hear the weight in your question. You're not asking for a tidy philosophical puzzle — you're naming something that feels like a real wound, maybe from something you've witnessed or experienced. I want to take that seriously rather than hand you a slogan.

Here's what I can offer from what these sources actually say, without pretending it resolves the ache:

**It's not a small or easily answered question, and Christian sources acknowledge that.** Cru puts it directly: "The Bible shows us that suffering actually points to (rather than disproves) the existence of a good God who cares about people" — but they're honest that these answers "can feel complex," not simple (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html).

**One thread: freedom and its cost.** EveryStudent addresses this almost exactly through the lens of a child being harmed. Their answer isn't that God causes it or is indifferent, but that "it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it... We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose." They push back on the idea that a good world requires God to override human freedom every time someone might choose evil (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html).

**Another thread: limited perspective.** thelife.com uses an analogy of a child undergoing painful surgery who can't understand why loving parents allow it: "the child's understanding is too limited to see why his parents allow his suffering... we are in no position to judge God" because we're "finite persons limited in time, space, intelligence, and insight" (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-2). I'll be honest — this one can feel like exactly the kind of "dodge" you're wary of, especially applied to something as raw as a suffering child. It's meant to humble our certainty that we've seen the whole picture, not to explain away the pain.

**What I think is the most substantive answer, though, is this one:** thelife.com argues that Christianity's distinct claim isn't an intellectual formula but that God "has done something about evil in the person of Jesus Christ... he did not just stay in heaven and say, 'OK you suckers, suffer!'" Instead, "he showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form... he suffered" — bearing punishment he didn't deserve. The claim is that God doesn't answer suffering from a distance but enters it (thelife, https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3).

I won't tell you that settles it — for many people it doesn't fully, and that's honest. Can I ask: is this coming from something specific you've seen happen, or is it more the general problem that's been sitting with you?

I'm really sorry about your dad. Losing a parent is one of the heaviest things we carry, and grief like this doesn't follow a tidy timeline — even a month later, the questions can feel just as raw as the day it happened.

I want to be honest with you: I don't have a source that gives a definitive answer about the eternal state of someone we don't know personally, especially without knowing what was in his heart. What I can share is what these sources say about how God relates to people and to grief:

- One writer describes how, before her mother died, "the Spirit of Christ was in her, that she belonged to him," and she died peacefully, trusting she'd "live forever with him" (*The Life*, [What Kind of Eternal Life Does Jesus Offer Us?](https://thelife.com/what-kind-of-eternal-life-does-jesus-offer-us)). That story centers on the person having consciously trusted Christ — I don't know if that was true for your dad, and I won't guess on your behalf.

- Another piece points to 2 Corinthians 5:8 — "We are of good courage, I say, and prefer rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with the Lord" — and reflects on Jesus telling the criminal on the cross that he'd be with Him "that very day in paradise," suggesting God's mercy toward those who turn to Him even at the very end (*The Life*, [Finally In His Presence](https://thelife.com/devotionals/finally-in-his-presence)).

- A Cru writer named Mel shares about her own father, who had never had a personal relationship with God until, near the end of his life, he prayed to receive Christ — and she found comfort afterward in Psalm 68:3-5, about God's commitment to those grieving loss (*Cru*, [Forgiving My Dad Set Us Both Free](https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/life-and-relationships/holidays/forgiving-my-dad-set-us-both-free.html)).

- Cru's own explainer on this topic says plainly that God offers a way to "know for sure where you'll spend eternity" through a relationship with Him — but that's framed as an invitation for the living, not a formula for judging someone else's fate (*Cru*, [What Happens When You Die?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-happens-when-you-die.html)).

None of these sources give me grounds to tell you definitively where your dad is now — and honestly, I don't think that's mine to say. What I can say is that not having gone to church isn't the same as never having reached toward God in some private, unseen way; only He knows what was in your dad's heart.

Can I ask — is it the not-knowing that weighs heaviest on you, or is there guilt mixed in too, like wishing you'd talked to him about faith before he passed? I'd like to understand what you're carrying.

It is completely understandable why this feels like a contradiction; it is one of the most mysterious and confounding parts of the Christian faith. To help explain it, Christians often make a distinction between "essence" and "person."

Here is a breakdown of what that means based on Christian teaching:

**1. One Essence (What God is)**
"Essence" refers to the "being" or the "what" of God. According to these sources, Christians believe there is only one divine essence (or one "being"). Because there is only one essence, there is only one God, not three separate gods (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity").

**2. Three Persons (Who God is)**
While there is only one essence, that one God eternally exists as three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity"). These are not just different "roles" or "masks" that God wears, but distinct individuals. For example, the Father is distinct from the Son because the Father sent the Son into the world (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity").

**Why it's not considered a contradiction**
The idea is that a contradiction would only occur if someone claimed God was three in the *same way* that He is one. However, because "essence" (what He is) and "person" (who He is) are different categories, Christians argue that God can be one in essence and three in person (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad").

**How to think about it**
Because humans are limited in their understanding and God is spirit and infinitely more complex than we are, many admit that human illustrations often fall short (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"). Some use mathematical analogies—suggesting that instead of $1+1+1=3$, it is more like $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").

Ultimately, this doctrine describes a God who is relational by nature, where the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have loved and interacted with one another for all eternity (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

It is completely understandable why that sounds like a contradiction. It is one of the most mysterious and "confounding" doctrines in the Christian faith (Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

The core idea is that Christians believe God is **one in essence** but **three in person**. To help make sense of this, it can be useful to look at how those two terms—essence and person—are used:

*   **Essence (What God is):** Essence refers to God's "being" or "substance." Christians believe there is only one God because there is only one divine essence or "being" (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad"). In mathematical terms, rather than thinking of it as $1+1+1=3$, some suggest it is more like $1 \times 1 \times 1 = 1$ (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?").
*   **Person (Who God is):** While there is only one essence, that essence exists eternally in three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

**Why it isn't considered a contradiction:**
The argument is that a contradiction would only exist if someone said God is three in the *same way* He is one. But because He is one in *essence* and three in *person*, the two truths are meant to coexist (Cru, "Entender la Trinidad"). 

The Bible shows these Persons are distinct through their relationships. For example, the Father sent the Son into the world, which indicates they are not the same person (Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief").

**A note on human understanding:**
Many people try to use analogies to explain this—like water having three forms (ice, liquid, steam) or the sun providing light, heat, and radiation—but most theologians agree that no human illustration is perfect and all fall short because humans are limited in their understanding, whereas God is infinite (EveryStudent, "What is the Holy Trinity?"; Cru, "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?").

Does that distinction between "who" God is and "what" God is help clarify things at all, or does it still feel a bit murky?

answers.text:
That's a really fair question — it does sound like a contradiction on the surface, but Christians would say it isn't, because it's not claiming God is three of the *same thing* and one of that *same thing* at the same time. Let me unpack it.

**The core claim: one "what," three "whos"**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief," the doctrine means "there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." Stated differently, "God is one in essence and three in person" ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

That distinction — *essence* vs. *person* — is the key to why it's not a logical contradiction. As Cru's Spanish-language article explains, "Dios es uno en forma diferente que es tres, [así] la Trinidad no es una contradicción. Sólo habría una contradicción si decimos que Dios es tres en la misma forma que él es uno" (God is one in a different way than he is three; there would only be a contradiction if we said God is three in the same way that he is one) ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

So the claim is: one essence (what God *is*), three persons (who God *is*) — not "one" and "three" of the identical thing.

**Why Christians believe this from the Bible**

Cru's article notes the Bible calls the Father God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit God (Acts 5:3-4) — yet also shows them as distinct from one another: "since the Father sent the Son into the world (John 3:16), He cannot be the same person as the Son," and after the Son returned to the Father, "the Father and the Son sent the Holy Spirit into the world (John 14:26; Acts 2:33)" ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

**A simple way it's sometimes put**

EveryStudent.com offers this: "If we were to use math, it would not be, 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1. God is a triune God... 'Tri' meaning three, and 'Unity' meaning one." They add that people have used illustrations like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam, or the sun giving light, heat, and radiation — while cautioning "no illustration is going to be perfect" ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

**Honest caveat**

Cru's piece on Jesus being God calls the Trinity "perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith," and admits "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding" ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)). So Christians aren't claiming to fully grasp it — they're saying it's *mysterious*, not *illogical*.

Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense as a starting point, or would it help to dig into one part more — like why they believe Jesus and the Spirit are called God in the first place?

It is a common point of conversation between people of these two faiths, as they both revere Jesus but view his identity in very different ways.

According to the provided materials, Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but is the Son of God and "God in the flesh" (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?").

While Muslims may view Jesus as a prophet, Christians emphasize that his role is radically different:
*   **His Identity:** Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?").
*   **His Work:** Fundamental to the Christian faith are the beliefs in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus from the dead, which are not believed by Muslims (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?").
*   **The Purpose:** From a Christian perspective, the focus is not on human efforts to reach God, but on God making a way for people to have a relationship with Him by sending His Son to die for human sins (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?").

Some who have explored these differences note that in the Bible, Jesus speaks with a level of authority that distinguishes him from a typical prophet (thelife, "The Life :: Seeking God Face to Face").

That is a very thoughtful question that gets to the heart of the fundamental differences between the two faiths.

While both Islam and Christianity revere many of the same figures—such as Abraham, Moses, and David—what is said about Jesus is "radically different" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html).

From a Christian perspective, the distinction is not just that Jesus was a prophet, but that he is the Son of God and "God in the flesh" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html). 

Some people who have explored this transition have noted a few specific reasons why they came to see Jesus as more than just a prophet:

*   **His Authority:** One person shared that when reading the Bible, they noticed Jesus did not speak like a typical prophet; instead, he "spoke with total authority" (thelife, https://thelife.com/seeking-god-face-to-face).
*   **The Crucifixion and Resurrection:** While Muslims do not believe in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus, Christians view these as "fundamental truths" of their faith (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html).

I hope this helps clarify the different perspectives. Is there a particular part of that distinction you'd like to explore more?

answers.text:
That's a really important question, and it touches the heart of the difference between the two faiths.

**The core difference**

According to Cru's article ["What Makes Christianity Different?"](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html), Muslims believe Jesus was a prophet but not God in the flesh, while Christians believe Jesus is "not only a prophet but the Son of God." The article also notes that Muslims don't accept the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus, whereas Christians see those as foundational truths of their faith.

**Why Christians say more than "prophet"**

EveryStudent's article ["Jesus in Islam"](https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html) addresses this respectfully, taking on the very question of "why not view Jesus as a prophet?" as one of the key questions Muslims often raise. It approaches this without criticizing Islam, but by pointing to what the Bible itself says about who Jesus claimed to be.

One personal account from a former Muslim on [The Life](https://thelife.com/seeking-god-face-to-face) describes reading the Bible and noticing something striking: "Jesus did not speak like a prophet. He spoke with total authority." That observation—that Jesus spoke and acted with a unique authority, forgiving sins, receiving worship, claiming oneness with the Father—is often the starting point Christians point to when explaining why they see him as more than a prophet: as God himself, come in the flesh, to make relationship with God possible not through human effort, but through what Jesus did on the cross and in his resurrection (as also described in the Cru article, citing John 3:16).

**A posture of respect, not just argument**

I'd also note that EveryStudent's approach here is worth highlighting: it says explicitly, "This article will be a very respectful presentation to anyone who wants to know about Jesus. No challenges. And there will be no criticism of any religion, in any way." That spirit seems like a good model — Christians engaging this question aren't trying to win a debate but to lovingly explain what they believe and why, while honoring the shared reverence for figures like Abraham, Moses, and Jesus that both faiths hold.

If you're wrestling with this question personally — whether from a Muslim background or just curious — I'm glad to explore it further with you. What's drawing you to ask?
